en: In the *Ādikarmapradīpa*: Om, homage to the Buddha!
Having bowed with devotion to the venerable Gurus, and to the Jinas together with their Sons;
This *Ādikarmapradīpa* is composed for those who seek its meaning;
it is written for the sake of the swift awakening of students,
and not out of competitive pride.
Therefore, all those whose suffering has been stilled ought to forgive me.
First, those mantras which were taught there for rites such as worship, etc., [are as follows].
Having drawn them together into a single collection, they are written down,
and not otherwise.
Having performed the cleansing of the mouth and other preliminary rites, one should likewise perform morning meditation and recitation.
One should recite the *Nāmasaṃgīti* and likewise make a formal aspiration (*praṇidhāna*).
Afterwards, having performed prostrations with the *Bhadracaryā* and other such prayers,
one should offer pure water free of living organisms to Jambhala according to the prescribed ritual.
One should likewise offer eight hundred handfuls of water to the deceased;
afterwards, one should perform the work of making clay stupas and so forth for the Buddhas and others.
Worship:
Having prepared a small mandala for the Guru and a mandala for one's chosen deity,
one should perform the recitation of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other such texts.
Having performed circumambulations of them as desired, and having made especially firm aspirations,
one should offer the *bali* offering to the Bodhisattvas for the long endurance of the Teaching.
With a joyful mind and well-composed, one should make aspirations; then, after first performing prostrations, one should finally dismiss the Buddhas and the gurus. 9 (1)

Furthermore, at the time of eating, one should offer the *bali* offering according to the ritual procedure with rice, condiments, and so forth, using the mantra dedicated to all elemental beings (*sarvabhautika*). One should present the food offering (*naivedya*) to the Three Jewels for three *ghaṭikās*.
One should eat according to the prescribed rule after first offering the seat of honor to the chosen deity;
then, having offered the morsel of food consisting of the remnants, one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana).
Having subsequently recited the verses on generosity and so forth, the wise one should dwell [there].
All the activities of a Bodhisattva should be performed with a joyful mind during the fourth watch;
furthermore, at the time of evening twilight, one should engage in the study of the True Dharma and other such practices. ||12-13||
Having paid homage with devotion through the five-limbed prostration to all the Jinas,
one should sleep upon the lion’s bed, joined with the yoga of the deity.
Upon rising, the ritual actions such as prostration and so forth should be performed once again.
This is considered the path for beginner beings.
For here, by a son of noble family or a daughter of noble family who has gained faith in the teaching of the Sugata—
First, one who goes for refuge to the Three Jewels should cultivate [this practice];
the benefits thereof were explained in detail by the Blessed One in the *Sūkarikāvadāna*. For it is said:
Those who go for refuge to the Buddha do not go to an evil rebirth;
having abandoned the human body, they obtain divine bodies.
"In this way, they go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha...
and so forth; and also in the *Triśaraṇānuśaṃsā-sūtra*:
In a single moment of mind, the merit arising from taking refuge is immeasurable;
it surpasses even the sins of those who are falsely accused, were they to exist for an entire day.
Therefore, if one desires the destruction of the substrates of existence, one should properly go for refuge to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, the supreme assembly.
Because of this statement,
the following procedure applies there: on an auspicious day...
A faithful son of good family or daughter of good family, being pure and clothed in clean garments,
[should place] an image of the Buddha in a secluded place.
Having performed worship with the five offerings,
one should offer maṇḍalakas before that [image] to the Three Jewels and to the Guru.
Having performed the offering of the ritual fee, with intense devotion he prostrated before the Three Jewels and at the feet of his teacher.
Standing either on his knees before [the teacher] or in a squatting position, he should do this three times.
One should make this request:
"O spiritual friend, grant me the three goings for refuge; [grant me] the status of a lay follower."
And the restraint of the minor training rules.
Then, having observed that the disciple has proceeded with a perfectly pure intention, the teacher should speak as follows.
"O long-lived one, say: 'I shall give according to my ability.'"
Pay heed, O Teacher: I, [name],
from this moment until I sit upon the seat of enlightenment, [take refuge].
To the Buddha, the Blessed One,
the all-knowing, the all-seeing.
The Great Being who has transcended all enmity and fear,
possessing an indestructible body and a supreme body.
I go for refuge to the supreme among bipeds; likewise,
I go for refuge to the Dharma, the best among those free from passion.
I go for refuge to the Saṅgha, the most excellent of assemblies.
Thus a second and a third time:
"O Teacher, please accept me who have gone for refuge to the Three."
Thus, the ten precepts of the Three Refuges should be conferred. They are as follows: Pay attention, O Teacher!
I, [name], from this moment until my sitting upon the seat of enlightenment;
I abstain from taking life. Likewise, I abstain from taking what is not given and from sexual misconduct.
False speech, slander, and harsh speech.
Frivolous speech,
covetousness,
and ill will.
Having abandoned wrong view, I abstain from wrong view. Thus a second and a third time.
One who has undertaken the ten precepts must maintain the restraint of a lay follower (*upāsaka*). In this regard, the formal ritual for that restraint is as follows:
Pay attention, Preceptor: just as those noble Arhats, for as long as life lasts, having abandoned the taking of life, abstained from taking life; [so may I].
In the same way, from this moment until the end of my life, having abandoned the taking of life, [I shall abstain] from the taking of life.
I abstain.
By this first limb, I shall train in accordance with and conform to the training of those noble Arhats.
I shall imitate.
Furthermore, just as those noble Arhats [abstain] for as long as life lasts from taking what is not given,
sexual misconduct, and false speech.
Abstaining from fermented liquor, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence;
even so, I, who am thus named, from this time forward—
For as long as life lasts, [one should abstain from] taking what is not given,
sexual misconduct, and false speech.
I abstain from fermented liquors, distilled spirits, and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence;
by this fifth limb, I...
In the training of those noble Arhats, I shall train after them, follow their example, and emulate them.
Thus a second and a third time: "It is appropriate; it is well. Thereafter—
Having refined [the disciple] through the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions, the verses on the six realms of existence,
the propitiation of sentient beings, the propitiation of the guru, and so forth,
he bestows grace by means of the empowerments.

One who has thus received the name of a lay follower (*upāsaka*), who has made the vow for the accomplishment of awakening, who has gone for refuge at the feet of the glorious guru, and who is endowed with faith— such a person should perform [the rite].
He now states what must be performed daily by one who desires the welfare of sentient beings.
However, all of this— beginning with the going for refuge— is not stated in the Root Sūtra;
likewise, there is no presentation of the Great [Sūtra].
Here he says: Even though we did not state this at the beginning for fear of excessive prolixity in the text, nevertheless all of this [is as follows].
For it has been stated by the wise that all this, beginning with meditative concentration, must be performed by a perfectly pure lay follower alone.
Not by anyone else.
Therefore, it has already been indicated that his training vows and so forth must be explained; thus, everything is complete.
It is well.
"Cleansing the mouth and so forth," etc.
At night, after the third watch.
According to the instruction:
having risen from his bed,
with palms joined and head bowed toward the surface of the earth.
One should speak thus:
"Oṃ, I perform prostration at the feet of all the Tathāgatas; [I perform prostration] at the body, speech, and mind of all the Tathāgatas."
By means of the ritual application: Oṃ, I offer myself for the service and worship of all Tathāgatas. Saka-
By means of the radiation of the vajras of body, speech, and mind from my own body within the noble dharmadhātu,
O Vajrasattva of all Tathāgatas,
please empower me!
Oṃ, I offer myself for the purpose of worship and consecration to all the Tathāgatas;
consecrate me with the vajra-jewel of all the Tathāgatas.
To me: Oṃ, I offer myself for the purpose of initiating the worship of all Tathāgatas.
O Vajradharma of all Tathāgatas...
Turn me [toward it].
Oṃ, for the sake of the ritual of worship to all Tathāgatas,
I offer myself.
Perform for me the vajra-activity of all the Tathāgatas.
I generate the vajra-mind of omniscience through the generation of the mind of equality with the vajra-wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
For the sake of pleasing the accomplishment of the nature of reality, which is the equality of the roots of virtue and the absence of conceptual proliferation;
and for the purpose of swiftly accumulating the two provisions.
"This procedure must be performed by the bodhisattva," because it is so stated in the *Vajraśikhara* and other tantras;
therefore, one should prostrate with the five limbs.
Having used a tooth-stick for the sake of clarity of the body and so forth.
Oṃ, O Pure Dharma, purify all my sins;
remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ!
One should perform the sprinkling with this handful of water consecrated by mantra. Then: Oṃ padma padma.
O auspicious one who draws forth the lotus, hūṃ 3!
One should wash one's face with water consecrated seven times; one will become beloved by all people, and no eye disease shall occur.
This king of mantras, which brings great benefits, is taught in the *Siddhaikavīra-tantra*.
Afterwards, upon a very soft seat in one's own meditation chamber, [one should visualize] one's chosen deity.
Having meditated at ease,
one should recite the mantra;
when weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra.
According to this statement,
one should thereafter recite the *Nāmasaṃgīti*, which compiles the essential reality of all the lords of sages.
"And the very vow" is connected with what follows:
preceded by vows such as the *Bhadracaryā*,
[one should offer] to all the Gurus, Buddhas, and Bodhisattvas.
The meaning is that one should perform a salutation.
He now states what is to be done immediately after sunrise: "pure water," which means water free from living organisms.
And so forth.
In the manner just described, one should offer water to Jambhala. Of what nature is it? Pure.
The purifier;
"devoid of living beings" according to the prescribed rule.
It has been examined. And thus it is said:

"When the vessel made of the hollow of the hand or a cup is full, and [the substance] has arisen from the secret place and so forth, the compassionate one should consume the liquid substance only after having examined it."
Moving upwards, downwards, and horizontally, performing steady contraction and circular motion,
and moving with the "cow's urine" (gomūtrikā) gait— such is the eightfold movement of living beings.
Thus, having completely restrained [the mind].

"According to the ritual procedure" means: according to the ritual procedure, [one should visualize] upon an eight-petaled lotus born from a red syllable *yaṃ* in front, [a form] born from a white syllable *āḥ*.
The moon disc, consisting of wisdom and skillful means,
is slightly red; upon it, together with the yellow stream of nectar from the syllable *jaṃ*, [is]—
He has a lotus [as his seat], wears a crown produced from jewels of golden color,
and is adorned with all ornaments.
With a protruding belly,
dwarf-like in form,
and wearing a garland of blue lotuses.
Having clearly visualized [this],
[place] Oṃ at the wrist of one's own right hand,
and Hūṃ in the middle of the hand.
Having clearly visualized *blūṃ* at the tips of all the fingers and *saḥ* at the bases of all the fingers, [recite] *oṃ*.
Having consecrated the hand with "Svāhā to Jambhala, Lord of Waters," [one should offer] the five nectars; in their absence, at least Akṣobhya.
Having drunk even a mere mouthful of water mixed with [the substance], one should utter "oṃ hūṃ blūṃ saḥ" and offer one hundred and eight mouthfuls of water.
He who gives with a steady mind and intense faith will, before long, become like Jambhala.
According to the word of the Blessed One: the fulfillment of the accumulations, and the ritual procedure for Jambhala and the water-giving [deities].
"To the departed" means:
in a clean place, [one should offer] "Oṃ, this water for all the departed."
Having uttered the mantra "svāhā," one hundred and eight handfuls of water should be offered. Thus [the rite for] the preta—
The procedure for the offering of water.
"Afterwards" refers to after the offering of water; "mud, caityas, and so forth" refers to the ritual actions and the like.
"Afterwards" means immediately following the offering of water.
The meaning is that one should construct a stūpa made of clay and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), all types of materials are included.
In this regard, the procedure for constructing the stūpa is as follows.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vairocanaprabharāja, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the perfectly enlightened Buddha.
It is as follows:
Oṃ, O subtle one, O peerless and equal one, O peaceful one, O self-controlled one!
O Yaśovatī, cross over to the unshakable, the supportless, the great refuge,
the undisturbed state of Nirvāṇa.
Svāhā! Blessed by the empowerment of all the Buddhas! By means of this dhāraṇī, [one should empower] a lump of clay or a lump of sand.
Having recited [the mantra] twenty-one times, one should fashion a caitya. As many atoms as there are in it, so many tens of millions of caityas are thereby fashioned. Following that—
Of those phenomena that arise from a cause, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa.
Having established oneself with this verse:
*Oṃ namo bhagavate puṣpaketurājāya tathā-*.
To the Arhat, the perfectly awakened Buddha, who has gone [to nirvana].
Namely: Oṃ puṣpa puṣpa mahāpuṣpa supuṣpa puṣpodbhava puṣpasaṃbhava puṣpavikrānta.
Puṣpavikīrṇa svāhā!
One should offer flowers consecrated with this dhāraṇī;
as many flowers as there are, that many tens of millions of flowers will have been offered.
Then: Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyak-saṃbuddha Ratnaketu-rāja.
To the Perfectly Awakened One.
Namely: Oṃ ratna ratna mahāratna ratnavijaya svāhā. By this—
One should perform the veneration of a shrine (caitya-vandanā). By the veneration of a single shrine, ten million shrine venerations are performed.
The ritual for the construction of a *caitya* is concluded.
Now, the ritual for striking all [the instruments] is being described.
Oṃ vasudhe svāhā. This is the mantra for taking the earth.
Oṃ vajradbhavāya svāhā. This is the mantra for Bimbabala.
Oṃ araja viraja svāhā. This is the mantra for anointing with oil. Oṃ.
Vajradhātugarbha svāhā. This is the mantra for casting the image.
Oṃ dharmadhātugarbha svāhā.
This is the mantra for casting the seal.
Oṃ vajramudgara ākoṭayati hūṃ phaṭ svāhā | This is the mantra for striking. Oṃ dharmarata svāhā |
The mantra for expulsion.
Oṃ supratiṣṭhitavajra svāhā; this is the mantra for installation.
Oṃ, blazing with the brilliance of the jewels of all the Tathāgatas, O womb of the dharmadhātu, svāhā!
The mantra for consecration: Oṃ svabhāvaviśuddha āhara (8) 2 āgaccha 3 dharmadhātugarbha svāhā.
The mantra for dismissal: Oṃ ākāśadhātugarbha svāhā. The mantra for requesting forgiveness: Then that...
One should install the *caitya* and other such items in a location free from harm.
This is the procedure for all striking rites.
"And the worship of the Buddha and others"— by the word "others," [are meant] Ārya Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Prajñāpāramitā, Tārā, and so forth.
The inclusion of Mārīcī and others [is intended].
In that regard, this is the sequence:
a variegated image and so forth.
One should wipe away what is unfit for bathing with peacock feathers and the like.
One should perform the bath with the mantra to be recited hereafter. In that regard: Oṃ Āḥ.
HŪṂ 2, for the sake of the perfect glory of the consecration of all Tathāgatas;
this is the bathing mantra: OṂ ĀḤ VAJRASAṂVARA HŪṂ SVĀHĀ.
Oṃ āḥ vajrasamālambana hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ vajravastra hūṃ svāhā | Oṃ āḥ vajrapuṣpa hūṃ svāhā |
Svāhā! Oṃ āḥ vajra-dhūpa hūṃ svāhā!
Oṃ āḥ vajra-dīpa hūṃ svāhā! Oṃ...
Āḥ vajra-naivedya hūṃ svāhā!
And whatever else there may be, all that as well—
One who knows the three principles should indeed offer [the oblation] to the mandala of the Guru, and so forth;
first, then, the mandala of the Guru.
One should perform [the rite];
afterwards, the other.
Why is the maṇḍala of the Guru presented at the very beginning?
Because of the statement: "For he is equal to all the Buddhas."
"From the scriptural statement, 'The Guru is the Buddha, and he is indeed the Dharma and the Saṅgha,' it is not so."

O Guru, all that has been stated by the Blessed One is for the purpose of demonstrating the excellence of one whose nature is free from delusion; it is not, however, for the sake of anything else herein.
The construction of the mandala by the expounder has been set forth in detail by the Blessed One in the *Śrīparamādibuddha*. (9)
At the beginning of the *Dharmacakrapravartana-tantra*:
"It is true; however, that [occurs] at the time of hearing the sublime Dharma."
It was taught with the intention that the Dharma should be heard with reverence;
it is not, however, as [some claim], for it has been stated [elsewhere] that one should listen at other times as well— three times a day— with supreme devotion, and so forth.
And it is said in the *Gurvārādhanā*:
"One should always give to the guru, and likewise, the Tathāgata should always be worshipped.
This is its meaning.
While a thing exists, one should joyfully give to the venerable feet of the illustrious Guru whatever object is desired by one's own mind; indeed,
whatever is most dear or even more distinguished.
For this has been stated in the continuous passage beginning with, "That indeed should be given to the guru," and so forth;
furthermore, if [the gift] is not available, he should provide that [which is available].
Because of this statement.
Having worshipped the four continents made of various jewels within the maṇḍala, one should offer them to the guru. By this—
From that arises the accumulation of merit; from that accumulation comes supreme enlightenment. Yet even that is unattached.
Is it not so for one who has gathered the two accumulations?
Liberation occurs.
How is it that one who is endowed with this very same accumulation of merit [attains it]?
It does not exist without the accumulation of knowledge,
because they are mutually dependent, like the wings of a bird upon the earth. (10)
Here it is said: the fulfillment of these two accumulations, merit and wisdom, occurs precisely through the fulfillment of the six perfections.
Through the creation of the maṇḍala of the gurus, these are fulfilled;
the qualities of being like the luster of gold, copper, and so forth are obtained. For it is thus:
Generosity consists of cow dung mixed with water; ethical discipline is thorough sweeping; patience is the removal of small ants; and vigor is—
The arousal of activity;
meditation is the making of the mind one-pointed at that very moment; wisdom is the blazing of the excellent lines.
Having constructed the maṇḍala of the Sage, one obtains these very six perfections.
He becomes golden-hued, liberated from all diseases,
distinguished among gods and men, with a radiance like the moon;
he is born into a royal lineage, enriched with wealth and gold.
Having performed bodily actions within this supreme abode of the Sugata.
I prepare the mandala.
"Having made a mandala for the Sage"—this is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa).
Having also made a mandala for the Guru, these qualities are obtained. Why? "One should not make any distinction between the Guru and Vajradhara."
Because of this statement: "In this regard as well, one should always practice generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, and so forth;
in a very short time, supreme enlightenment is attained."
Thus, everything is well-established.
In this regard, the procedure for the maṇḍala of the gurus is as follows: *oṃ āḥ hūṃ*—having performed the yoga of the place and oneself...
The Rakṣas: "Oṃ Hrīṃ Svāhā"—having thus performed the washing of hands and sipping of water;
"Oṃ Hūṃ."
Having occupied the seat, one performs the consecration of the ground with: *oṃ āḥ vajrabhūme hūṃ*.
(11) *Oṃ*... [end of line]
"O Vajrasattva, dispel all obstacles! HŪṂ PHAṬ! Having thus consecrated cow dung and other materials with this mantra, one should prepare a maṇḍalaka in a clean place. OṂ ĀḤ.
Having consecrated it with "Vajrarekhe hūṃ," take up the empowered flower and [recite] "Oṃ."
Having offered a flower in the center with the mantra "O excellent Vajra-guru, accept this respectful arghya, svāhā," one should wash one's hands.
Then, in the center, there is a square [mountain] adorned with eight peaks,
its eastern, southern, western, and northern sides being constructed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, and gold respectively.
He fashioned Mount Sumeru out of the four jewels;
in its center, upon a lion throne inlaid with various gems, [he sat].
The venerable Guru-Bhaṭṭāraka, who possesses the splendor of the interior of a blooming eight-petaled lotus and is adorned with various ornaments.
Having seen [him] standing in the playful grace of Vajrasattva,
then, to the east of Sumeru, [there is] a half-moon shape.
Śukla is Pūrvavideha;
in the south is Jambudvīpa, triangular and golden-colored.
In the west, Aparagodānīya is circular and red;
in the north, it is square—
Having visualized Śrāṃ as dark-complexioned Uttarakuṛu,
one should visualize each of these as a lotus.
He scattered [offerings] consisting of ruby, sapphire, lapis lazuli, red diamond, pearl, and coral;
then, having removed the flower previously offered, he recited: *oṃ hūṃ*.
One should offer a flower in the center with the words, "Homage to the Middle Guru," and then [offer it] with "Oṃ Vajragurave."
The word "namas" is placed above that.
Oṃ yaṃ, homage to Pūrvavideha. Oṃ raṃ, homage to Jambudvīpa. Oṃ.
Laṃ, homage to Aparagodānīya;
Oṃ vaṃ, homage to Uttarakuru. [These are] in the directions starting from the east.
Oṃ, homage to the island of Dehavideha. Oṃ ra, homage to the island of Ambara.
Oṃ lā, homage to the island of Kurukaurava. Oṃ vā, homage to the island of Śākhottaramañjarī.
In the intermediate directions beginning with the southeast:
Oṃ ya gajar [atn] āya namaḥ.

Oṃ ra, homage to the jewel of the man (puruṣaratna)! Oṃ la, homage to the jewel of the horse (aśvaratna)! Oṃ va, homage to the jewel of the woman (strīratna)! Thus [it is said] between Sumeru and Jambūdvīpa.
In the directions beginning with the east: Oṃ yāḥ khaḍgaratnāya namaḥ;
Oṃ rāḥ maṇiratnāya namaḥ.
Oṃ lāḥ, homage to the wheel-jewel. Oṃ vāḥ, homage to all treasures.
Thus for the intermediate directions: Oṃ Aḥ, homage to Candra;
Oṃ Āḥ, homage to Sūrya.
One should offer flowers on the western and eastern sides of Mount Sumeru.
And all these, having been produced from their respective seeds, must be offered to the Guru.
Then, having visualized [the deities] as being filled with various jewels while holding a handful of flowers:
"Homage to you! Homage to you! Homage to you! Homage!"
Homage!
Out of devotion, I bow to you, O Lord Guru; be gracious to me.
Having recited thus,
one performs the prostration with the mantra: *oṃ sarvatathāgatapādavandanāṃ karomi*.
"One should perform" refers to the procedure for constructing the maṇḍala of the Guru.
"Worship of one's chosen deity" is as follows:
Oṃ Āḥ Vajrabhūme Hūṃ.
Having recited, beginning with "Oṃ surekhe sarvatathāgatā adhiṣṭhantu svāhā," over the mandala...
Having offered a flower and washed one's hands, [recite]:
*oṃ maṇidhari vajriṇi mahāpratisare*.
One should perform self-protection by scattering a flower on the region of one's own head while reciting the mantra: *rakṣa 2 māṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*.
Thereafter, having likewise visualized the continents of Sumeru, one should worship one's chosen deity upon them according to the oral instructions. Five.
The three bodies of the Tathāgatas and the Tathāgatas themselves are on the side of the Tathāgatas: HŪṂ OṂ TRĀṂ HRĪḤ.
They are transformed from the syllable Khaṃ; they are blue, white, yellow, red, and green; and they wear monastic robes and ushnishas.
The earth-touching, enlightenment, boon-granting, meditative,
and fear-dispelling mudrās; all [of these], with the exception of Vairocana.
They are seated upon sun-thrones and possess the radiance of the sun; Vairocana, however, is seated upon a moon-throne and possesses the radiance of the moon.
In the corners, from the syllables *laṃ*, *vaṃ*, *raṃ*, and *yaṃ*, which are yellow, white, red, and smoke-colored respectively,
[arises] a square...

Above the maṇḍalas of the four great elements, which are circular, triangular, and semicircular in shape, there are Yoginīs adorned with many ornaments, situated upon moons in the directions beginning with the southeast.
[The goddesses] Śvetā, Indrāṇī, Nīlā,
Saṃkāsā, Raktā, Śyāmalā, and Viṣahā arise from the syllables LĀṂ, MĀṂ, YĀṂ, and BHĀṂ.
Having correctly visualized [them] as consisting of earth, water, fire, and wind,
and as holding a wheel, a thunderbolt, blood-red water, and a lotus respectively;
Or, because there is no difference between the mantra and the deity, one should worship the seed-syllable in its proper place.
Then one should present the five qualities of sensual pleasure;
one should always worship the Buddhas with the five qualities of sensual pleasure according to the ritual procedure.
By means of these five types of symbolic worship, one shall swiftly attain Buddhahood.
Thus, from the words of the *Śrīsamāja*.

Thus, for these [deities] beginning with Akṣobhya, respectively, there is the sound of the lute and so forth in the form of their bodies, the appearance of lamps and so forth, the fragrance of sandalwood and so forth, the taste of milk and so forth, and [the touch of] garments and so forth—
One should give what is to be touched. Therefore, even when the object is not present, everything is to be accomplished through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Because of the statement:
"In other cases as well, a great mental worship must be performed.
But surely, by means of the mind?
